text.p: Romania's Sports Minister ordered an inquiry on Friday into allegations of financial irregularities and match-rigging by the country's soccer federation over the past four years.
"A special Sports Ministry commission will investigate alleged financial irregularities by the FRF (Romanian Soccer Federation)," Sorin Stanescu said.
"If confirmed, these allegations will cast a shadow not only on Romanian soccer but all Romanian sport."

The inquiry was ordered in response to a series of accusations by club officials that the FRF was siphoning off "fees" for foreign transfers of Romanian players. Some officials alleged the federation was behind systematic match-rigging.
Federation President Mircea Sandu has denied the allegations, saying any involvement by government or parliament would be tantamount to interference in the sport's internal matters.
"FIFA and UEFA rules ban political interference in our affairs. We will be in danger of being banned by soccer's governing bodies if political interference continues in soccer," Sandu said last week.
"Politicians want to take control of soccer. This shows a misunderstanding of the laws under which the FRF functions."

Marcel Puscas, president of Romania's most prestigious club Steaua Bucharest, has led the charge against the federation, accusing it of skimming off 10 percent of each transfer fee since 1991, a year after the fall of communism. He has also demanded closer government scrutiny of FRF accounts.
The federation last week banned Puscas from involvement in the sport for a year for "defamatory statements."
Steaua Bucharest, Universitatea Craiova, Universitatea Cluj and other top clubs have asked the FRF to return money taken for the transfers. Steaua say they alone have paid out $920,000.
The federation says such practices are normal, with funds being used to train young players.
Dumitru Sechelariu, mayor of the eastern city of Bacau and president of first division FC Bacau, last week demanded a parliamentary inquiry into the federation's "illegitimacy".
"Any citizen...has the right to lodge appeals in court, but FRF regulations do not allow this," Sechelariu said in a letter to parliament. "The FRF wants to try all crimes itself."

A series of rigging allegations have been rejected by federation tribunals in the past three years for lack of evidence. National coach Anghel Iordanescu quit for a time last year in protest against what he said was routine fixing.
